name: Perseverance (Mars 2020)
short_status: Operating as of 26 October 2026, and the record holder for distance driven on another world. On sol 2006, 11 October 2026, a 91.31 m drive took its odometer to 45.22 km, past the 45.16 km Opportunity set, and JPL announced the record the next day. NASA's raw-image feed carries pictures taken through sol 2020, the latest at 05:30 UTC on 26 October 2026, and its traverse file, last modified 15 October 2026, ends on sol 2009 at 45,223.649 m.
tagline: NASA · United States · Rover · 2021 · Multipolar Mars Operating
stats: driven by sol 2009, read straight from NASA's Mars 2020 traverse file on 26 October 2026 (last modified 15 October), the furthest any vehicle has driven on another world
sample tubes filled in NASA's published sample table as it stood on 3 September 2026, ten of them left on the ground at the Three Forks depot in January 2023
of oxygen MOXIE made from Martian carbon dioxide across 16 runs before NASA retired it in 2023

facts.label: Launch and landing
facts.value: Launched 30 July 2020 at 11:50 UTC (7:50 a.m. EDT) on a United Launch Alliance Atlas V 541 from Space Launch Complex 41, Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida, for a 471 million km crossing. Touchdown was 18 February 2021 at 20:55 UTC (3:55 p.m. EST), 3:53 p.m. local mean solar time at the landing site. One-way light time that day was 11 minutes 22 seconds, so the entire descent was autonomous.

facts.label: The off-Earth distance record
facts.value: Perseverance holds it. On 11 October 2026, sol 2006, its odometer reached 28.10 miles (45.22 km), passing the 28.06 miles (45.16 km) NASA gives as Opportunity's final odometry, and JPL announced on 12 October that it had driven further than any vehicle on the surface of another world. A 91.31 m drive that sol did it. NASA's traverse file, last modified 15 October 2026, agrees: its sol 1980 drive ends at 45,126.078 m and its sol 2006 drive at 45,217.391 m, so the record fell partway through that drive. On the way the rover also passed the 35.7 km that Apollo 17's astronauts drove on the Moon and the total for Lunokhod 2, which JPL gives as 39 km and a Russian remapping of its tracks puts at about 42 km. It covered the distance in five and a half years; Opportunity took almost 15.

facts.label: Masses and size
facts.value: About 1,025 kg on Earth and 393 kg on Mars, including a 45 kg turret on a 2.1 m robotic arm. The body is roughly 3 m long, 2.7 m wide and 2.2 m tall, not counting the arm.

facts.label: Power
facts.value: One Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator supplied by the US Department of Energy, producing about 110 watts from the decay of plutonium-238, with two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries for peak demand.

facts.label: Science payload
facts.value: 59 kg (130 pounds) in seven instruments: Mastcam-Z, the Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA), the Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment (MOXIE), the Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry (PIXL), the Radar Imager for Mars' Subsurface Experiment (RIMFAX), SHERLOC and SuperCam.

facts.label: Cameras and microphones
facts.value: The press kit counts 25 cameras flown to Mars on the mission, 23 on the spacecraft and 2 on Ingenuity, and calls that the most ever flown on a deep-space mission. Nineteen are on the rover itself. There are two microphones: a commercial off-the-shelf part on a port-side panel for entry, descent and landing, and one built into SuperCam.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: NASA states approximately $2.4 billion to build and launch the Mars 2020 Perseverance mission, plus approximately $300 million to land the rover and operate it through the prime mission.

facts.label: Prime mission versus actual
facts.value: The prime mission was one Mars year, about 687 Earth days, which ran out in early January 2023, per the Mars 2020 landing press kit. NASA's Mars 2020 raw-image feed, queried on 26 October 2026, shows the rover had reached sol 2020 that day, almost three Mars years and more than five and a half Earth years after landing. JPL said on 12 October 2026 that NASA had approved the mission's first extension, which began that October and runs through roughly the end of 2028.

facts.label: Traverse, as measured today
facts.value: NASA's M20_waypoints.json, read again on 26 October 2026 (last modified 15 October 2026), holds 706 waypoints and ends at sol 2009 with a cumulative odometry of 45,223.649 m (45.22 km). On 9 October 2026 it held 703 waypoints and ended at sol 1980 with 45,126.078 m. Downloaded on 3 September 2026 it held 700 waypoints running from sol 13 to sol 1965, with a final cumulative odometry of 45,105.717 m (45.11 km). Every one of the 700 waypoints carries exactly one attached panorama. The same file read on 23 August 2026 ended at 697 waypoints, sol 1955 and 44,976.465 m, and a week before that at 694 waypoints, sol 1947 and 44,967.045 m; those rows are all still in the file, and every reading is correct for its date.

facts.label: Out-driving Curiosity
facts.value: The equivalent Curiosity file, read on 26 October 2026, ends at 38,480.16 m after 1,386 waypoints and 5,045 sols. Lining the two files up date by date, using the standard sol-to-UTC conversion from each landing, Perseverance's odometer passed Curiosity's around 20 June 2025 at roughly 35.6 km, having landed eight and a half years later. That comparison is azmth's own computation from the two published files. NASA does not state it.

facts.label: Elevation, and the climb out of Jezero
facts.value: The traverse file puts the landing site at -2,569.91 m on the areoid, the lowest point of the whole traverse at -2,585.87 m on sol 153, and the highest at -1,786.00 m on sol 1354, which falls around 10 December 2024. That climb of 799.87 m matches the 800 m rim-to-crest ascent NASA quotes for the summit of the crater rim in December 2024. The last waypoint in the file on 26 October 2026, sol 2009, sits at -1,937.45 m.

facts.label: Sample tubes
facts.value: The rover carried 43 tubes: 38 for samples and 5 witness tubes preloaded to record what the sampling hardware itself brought from Earth. On 3 September 2026 NASA's public sample table showed 30 of 38 filled and 3 of 5 witness tubes sealed, the newest entry being a core called Gallants from Salmon Point, listed with its sealing sol as TBD; the table's photograph of the Gallants target was taken on sol 1551 (1 July 2025). No later sample had been published by 26 October 2026, and JPL's release of 12 October 2026 counts 29 rock and regolith samples, which with the atmospheric Roubion tube makes the same 30.

facts.label: The Three Forks depot
facts.value: Ten tubes were laid on the ground about 5 to 15 m apart at a flat spot called Three Forks: igneous cores, sedimentary cores, one atmospheric sample and one witness tube. JPL reports confirmation that the tenth and last tube was down arriving about 5 p.m. PST on Sunday 29 January 2023 (01:00 UTC on 30 January), less than six weeks after construction began. The depot is a backup, in case Perseverance itself cannot hand its collection over.

facts.label: MOXIE
facts.value: Sixteen runs, 122 grams of oxygen in total, at up to 12 grams an hour and 98 percent purity or better. The first run, on sol 60 (20 April 2021), made about 5.4 grams after a two-hour warm-up, working at roughly 800 degrees Celsius. The final run was on 7 August 2023 and NASA announced the retirement on 6 September 2023.

facts.label: The microphones, and two speeds of sound
facts.value: SuperCam's microphone records pressure fluctuations from 20 Hz to 12.5 kHz at a 25 kHz sampling rate, and up to 50 kHz in a 100 kHz mode. The Nature study covering sols 1 to 216 reports 4 hours 40 minutes of Martian sound recorded, 46 percent of it atmospheric turbulence. Maurice et al. found that the speed of sound at the surface differs by about 10 m/s either side of 240 Hz, a consequence of carbon dioxide vibrational relaxation at low pressure: 237.7 plus or minus 3 m/s below the threshold, derived from Ingenuity's 84.43 Hz blade-passage tone, and 246 to 257 m/s above it from laser-induced sparks. Popular accounts round these to 240 and 250 m/s.

facts.label: The potential biosignature
facts.value: Perseverance cored the rock Cheyava Falls in the Bright Angel formation on sol 1215 (21 July 2024) and sealed the core as Sapphire Canyon, sample 25. PIXL found vivianite (a hydrated iron phosphate) and greigite (an iron sulfide) in leopard-spot patterns. A paper led by Joel Hurowitz of Stony Brook University appeared in Nature on 10 September 2025; NASA calls the result a potential biosignature, defined by the agency as a substance or structure that might have a biological origin but requires more data before any conclusion about life can be reached.

timeline: Launch at 11:50 UTC on an Atlas V 541 from Complex 41, Cape Canaveral, with the Ingenuity helicopter folded flat against the rover's belly.

Landing at 20:55 UTC in Jezero crater. Range Trigger opened the 21.5 m parachute at about 11 km on distance-to-target rather than speed; the Lander Vision System matched camera images to an onboard map between roughly 4.2 and 2.2 km altitude, fixing position to about 40 m in under ten seconds, and the descent stage was free to move the touchdown point by up to 600 m.

First drive, 6.5 m in 33 minutes on sol 13. NASA names the touchdown spot Octavia E. Butler Landing, for the Pasadena science-fiction writer who was the first of her field to win a MacArthur Fellowship.
Two firsts on consecutive days. Ingenuity flies on sol 58, and on sol 60 MOXIE pulls about 5.4 grams of oxygen out of the Martian atmosphere.

The first coring attempt returns an empty tube: the rock crumbled to powder. The tube is sealed anyway and appears in NASA's sample table as sample 1, Roubion, classified atmospheric. The first rock core, Montdenier, is sealed on sol 194.

Nature publishes the first characterisation of the Martian acoustic environment, built from SuperCam and EDL microphone recordings, reporting two speeds of sound about 10 m/s apart across a 240 Hz threshold.

Perseverance builds the first sample depot on another world at Three Forks, setting ten tubes on the ground about 5 to 15 m apart so a future lander could collect them without the rover. JPL confirms the tenth tube is down at about 5 p.m. PST on Sunday 29 January, less than six weeks after construction began.

MOXIE's sixteenth and last run. NASA announces the instrument's retirement with a career total of 122 grams of oxygen and a best rate of 12 grams an hour, which is the figure NASA calls twice its original goal for the instrument.
Sol 1215: the rover cores Cheyava Falls in the Bright Angel formation and seals the sample as Sapphire Canyon.

The crater rim campaign. Perseverance climbs out of Jezero, a rim-to-crest ascent of about 800 m, summiting in December 2024. The traverse file's highest waypoint, -1,786.00 m, falls on sol 1354, around 10 December.

Nature publishes Hurowitz et al. on the vivianite and greigite in Cheyava Falls. NASA describes the finding as a potential biosignature and points at its Confidence of Life Detection scale rather than claiming a detection.

On sol 1762 the rover fixes its own position on Mars for the first time without human help, matching a navcam panorama to onboard orbital imagery at a featureless spot called Mala Mala, using the processor it once used to talk to Ingenuity. On sol 1890 (14 June 2026) the odometer passes a marathon, 42.195 km, five years and four months after landing; Opportunity took eleven years and two months to cover the same ground. Its sol 1980 drive (15 September 2026) leaves it about 34 m short of Opportunity's record, and raw images arrive from sol 1988 on 23 September 2026.

Sol 2006: a 91.31 m drive takes the odometer to 45.22 km, past the 45.16 km Opportunity set, and JPL announces the next day that Perseverance has driven further than any vehicle on the surface of another world. The mission's first extension begins the same month and runs to roughly the end of 2028.

images.caption: PIA26344, a Perseverance self-portrait made from 62 WATSON frames taken on 23 July 2024, with the arrowhead-shaped rock nicknamed Cheyava Falls lying to the left of the rover near the centre of the picture.

PIA24428, a still frame from video shot by a downward-looking camera on the descent stage as Perseverance was lowered on the sky crane's cables toward the floor of Jezero crater on 18 February 2021, with dust raised by the descent engines around the rover.

The United Launch Alliance Atlas V 541 lifting off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station on 30 July 2020 at 7:50 a.m. EDT, carrying Perseverance and the Ingenuity helicopter, seen from the Atlas Space Operations Center.

PIA25212, a Mastcam-Z panorama of 64 frames taken on 11 April 2022, sol 406, looking out across the fan-shaped river delta on the western side of Jezero crater, with sand bedforms running along its base. NASA states that the colour bands have been processed to accentuate differences and that the sky would not look blue to a human standing there.

PIA24203, the gold-plated Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment photographed after installation inside Perseverance's body before launch, with the wide intake tube for filtered Martian carbon dioxide on its top surface.

PIA24832, a Mastcam-Z image taken on 4 September 2021 looking into the drill to confirm that a rock core had been retained inside the sample tube held there, the core later sealed as the sample Montdenier.
